primitives.name: Perceptron Convergence Theorem
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 2 (Perceptron Convergence Theorem). Suppose the perceptron algorithm is run on a linearly separable data set D with margin γ > 0. Assume that ||x|| ≤1 for all x ∈D. Then the algorithm will converge after at most 1 γ2 updates.
primitives.latex: w^{(k)} = w^{(k-1)} + yx \;\; \text{if } y\,w^{(k-1)}\!\cdot x < 0, \qquad k_{\max} \le \frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: w^(k) in R^D: weight vector after k-th update (units inverse to feature units so w.x is a dimensionless score); x in R^D: feature vector with ||x||<=1 (normalized, dimensionless); y in {-1,+1}: binary label (dimensionless); gamma>0: geometric margin, dimensionless under unit-norm convention, gamma = min_n y_n w*.x_n / ||w*||; k_max: number of perceptron updates (dimensionless integer count); 1/gamma^2: dimensionless upper bound on update count. w.x is a dimensionless score, so the bound is dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: Data set D linearly separable with margin gamma>0; all examples have norm ||x||<=1; binary labels y in {-1,+1}; update w<-w+yx applied only on misclassified examples (y w.x<0); the stated theorem uses the no-bias variant (b=0).
primitives.breakdown_regime: No finite bound when data are not linearly separable (gamma=0 makes 1/gamma^2 diverge); the perceptron then cycles forever. Vacuous as gamma->0 (near-degenerate margins give astronomically large update budgets). Without the unit-norm assumption the bound becomes R^2/gamma^2 with R=max||x||. Noisy or non-separable labels violate the premise entirely.

primitives.name: Bayes Optimal Classifier and Bayes Error Rate
primitives.verbatim_quote: We can deﬁne the Bayes optimal classiﬁer as the classiﬁer that, for any test input ˆx, simply returns the ˆy that maximizes computeD( ˆx, ˆy), or, more formally: f (BO)( ˆx) = arg max ˆy∈Y D( ˆx, ˆy) (2.1)
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: D(x,y): data-generating probability distribution over X x Y; D(x-hat,y-hat) a conditional probability (dimensionless, in [0,1], sums to 1 over y for fixed x); f^(BO): Bayes optimal classifier, map X->Y; x-hat in X: test input; y-hat in Y: candidate label; argmax over y-hat in Y selects the label of maximal conditional probability; 1 - D(x,f^(BO)(x)): per-input zero/one error probability (dimensionless, [0,1]); the Bayes error rate is the expectation of this per-input error over x~D (dimensionless probability). All quantities are probability measures, dimensionless and homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: Access to the true data-generating distribution D over (x,y) in X x Y (an oracle computeD); zero/one loss; comparison restricted to deterministic classifiers (the text notes a stronger randomized-classifier result also holds); discrete labels; D(x,.) a valid conditional probability mass function.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Unusable in practice because D is unknown; learning exists precisely because no one hands you D. Optimality holds only under zero/one loss; under squared or absolute loss the argmax-of-D rule is not optimal. Ties in the argmax make the classifier non-unique. If D is misspecified or the i.i.d. assumption fails the guarantee dissolves. The Bayes error is a lower bound, not achievable from finite samples.

primitives.name: Loss of SupervisedIL (T-squared compounding-error bound)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 18 (Loss of SupervisedIL). Suppose that one runs Algo- rithm 18.1 using a multiclass classiﬁer that optimizes the 0-1 loss (or an upperbound thereof). Let ϵ be the error rate of the underlying classiﬁer (in expectation) and assume that all instantaneous losses are in the range [0, ℓ(max)]. Let f be the learned policy; then:
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: tau: trajectory (sequence of observation/action/loss triples), dimensionless combinatorial object; f: learned policy (observations->actions); ell_t: instantaneous loss at step t in [0,ell^(max)] (abstract cost units); sum_t ell_t: total trajectory loss (cost units); E_{tau~f}[.]: expectation over trajectories induced by policy f (cost units); ell^(max): upper bound on instantaneous loss (cost units); T: time horizon / trajectory length (dimensionless integer count); epsilon: expected zero/one error rate of the base multiclass classifier (dimensionless probability in [0,1]). The term ell^(max) T^2 epsilon has cost units, matching the left-hand side; dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: Multiclass classifier optimizes 0-1 loss (or an upper bound thereof); epsilon is the classifier's expected error rate; all instantaneous losses bounded in [0,ell^(max)]; fixed horizon T; training only on the expert-visited state distribution (no recovery data); the bound is worst-case over the compounding-error construction.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The T^2 factor is tight in the worst case (Theorem 19 lower bound, p.215, grows like T^2 epsilon for small epsilon), so it cannot be improved for SupervisedIL in general. It is loose by a factor T relative to the hopeful ell^(max) T epsilon. It ceases to be a useful guarantee when epsilon >= 1/T (then T^2 epsilon >= T, loss can exceed the whole horizon); the text flags 'if epsilon >= 1/T, we lose.' A bad expert caps achievable performance. The bound assumes the learner never sees off-expert states, which is exactly its failure mode (compounding error).

primitives.name: Loss of DAgger (linear-T bound via dataset aggregation)
primitives.verbatim_quote: Theorem 20 (Loss of Dagger). Suppose that one runs Algorithm 18.3 using a multiclass classiﬁer that optimizes the 0-1 loss (or an upperbound thereof). Let ϵ be the error rate of the underlying classiﬁer (in expectation) and assume that all instantaneous losses are in the range [0, ℓ(max)]. Let f be the learned policy; then:
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: Same symbols as p3 (tau, f, ell_t, ell^(max), T, epsilon; cost units for loss terms, dimensionless for T and epsilon) plus: MaxIter: number of DAgger iterations (dimensionless integer count); O(ell^(max) T log T / MaxIter): remainder term in cost units, vanishing when MaxIter >= T log T. The key structural difference from Eq (18.2) is a single power of T rather than T^2. Every term carries cost units; dimensionally homogeneous.
primitives.assumptions: Same as SupervisedIL (0-1-loss classifier, expected error epsilon, losses in [0,ell^(max)], horizon T) PLUS an interactive expert queryable on learner-visited states; dataset aggregation (train on the union of all rounds' data); the returned f is the best of the MaxIter policies selected on held-out development tasks; the O(.) remainder requires MaxIter large (>= T log T). The stronger Eq (18.5), loss <= expert + ell^(max) T epsilon + O(epsilon), additionally requires the loss to be strongly convex in f and MaxIter = O-tilde(T/epsilon).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The linear-T guarantee degrades if MaxIter is too small (the remainder O(ell^(max) T log T / MaxIter) dominates). DAgger can be unstable and non-monotone across iterations, so blindly using the final policy fails; selection on held-out tasks is required. It needs an interactive expert (a much stronger demand than passive trajectories); if the expert cannot be queried on off-policy states the method reverts toward SupervisedIL's T^2 behavior. The strongly-convex variant's O(epsilon) term needs strong convexity, which 0-1 loss does not satisfy (only its convex surrogates do).

layer2.mapping: Eq (18.4) is structurally isomorphic to Eq (18.2) (primitive p3): both are E_{tau~f}[sum ell] <= E_{tau~expert}[sum ell] + ell^(max) T^k epsilon (+ remainder). The isomorphism maps k=2 -> k=1 and adds a vanishing O(ell^(max) T log T / MaxIter) remainder. The structural operator implementing the map is dataset aggregation: re-weighting the training distribution from expert-visited states to learner-visited states removes exactly one factor of T, the compounding-error horizon. In the 22-player football dynamical system this binds to the transition kernel over game states: a Coach-Mind policy trained only on expert (successful historical drive) states compounds errors when it drifts into off-distribution states (e.g. 3rd-and-long after a sack); DAgger-style aggregation rehearses recovery from the learner's own visited states, collapsing quadratic drive-collapse risk to linear. The state variable is the visited-state distribution; the constraint is expert queryability; the info channel is the expert's recovery-action label.
layer2.telemetry: Calibrating observables: per-step classifier error epsilon (held-out action-prediction error), horizon T (steps per drive/trajectory), max instantaneous loss ell^(max) (worst single-play cost), DAgger iteration count MaxIter, and the empirical gap between expert-visited and learner-visited state distributions (covariate shift / dA-distance). The T^2->T reduction is verified by measuring trajectory loss vs T on held-out drives: slope proportional to T^2 for SupervisedIL vs proportional to T for DAgger. No sportsbook odds used.

reasoning_traces.think:
This extraction treats Daume's A Course in Machine Learning as a source of sovereign learning-theoretic invariants, not as a prompt for sports analogy. Four primitives were pulled with verbatim theorem statements and exact source notation: the Perceptron Convergence Theorem (p.50), the Bayes Optimal Classifier (p.19), the SupervisedIL T-squared compounding-error bound (Theorem 18, p.214), and the DAgger linear-T bound (Theorem 20, p.217). The first three are Layer-1 source invariants; the fourth carries the Layer-2 [ISOMORPHISM] that binds the pair of imitation-learning bounds into a single structural kernel.

Begin with the perceptron. The theorem is a finite mistake-bound: under linear separability with margin gamma greater than zero and unit-norm examples, the number of updates is at most one over gamma squared. The proof is a two-sided squeeze on the angle between the learned weight w and the unknown separator w-star: the projection w-star dot w grows by at least gamma per update, because every update is on a misclassified example and w-star has margin gamma, while the norm of w grows by at most one per update, because the examples are unit-norm and the update adds y times x. Alignment therefore must increase, and since alignment is bounded above by one, the process terminates. The dimensional content is clean: w dot x is a dimensionless score, gamma is a dimensionless margin under the unit-norm convention, and one over gamma squared is a dimensionless count. The breakdown regime is the singularity gamma tending to zero: the bound diverges, and for non-separable data the perceptron never converges. This is not a defect of the theorem but its honest boundary; it says nothing about the non-separable case, which is precisely why the book later introduces slack variables and the support vector machine.

The Bayes optimal classifier is the complementary ceiling. Given the true distribution D, the Bayes classifier returns the label maximizing D of x-hat and y-hat, and it achieves minimal zero-one error among deterministic classifiers; the per-input error is one minus D of x and the Bayes label. This is a population-level invariant: it is the best any learner could do, and it is unattainable from finite samples because D is never handed to us. The two primitives bracket learning from opposite ends. The perceptron gives a finite-sample convergence guarantee under a separability assumption, while Bayes gives the asymptotic error floor under no assumption beyond knowing D. The gap between them is the entire subject of statistical learning theory: inductive bias, estimation error, and approximation error.

The imitation-learning pair is where the structural isomorphism lives. Theorem 18 bounds the loss of a policy learned by pure supervised imitation: the expected total trajectory loss under the learned policy is at most the expected total loss under the expert, plus ell-max times T squared times epsilon. Theorem 20 bounds DAgger: the same left-hand side and expert term, but ell-max times T times epsilon, plus a remainder of order ell-max times T log T over MaxIter. Reading these as the same kernel with a single exponent changed, T squared to T, is the [ISOMORPHISM]. The operator that implements the exponent reduction is dataset aggregation: instead of training on the expert's visited-state distribution, DAgger trains on the learner's own visited states, labeled by the expert. One factor of T is exactly the compounding-error horizon: a single early mistake shifts the state distribution, and under SupervisedIL every subsequent step is now off-distribution, so errors multiply across the horizon. By matching the training distribution to the deployment distribution, DAgger removes one power of T. The lower bound in Theorem 19 (p.215) shows T squared times epsilon is unavoidable for SupervisedIL, so the isomorphism is not a loose rewriting; it is a tight structural separation.

Dimensional homogeneity holds throughout: every term in both bounds carries units of loss, a cost; epsilon is a dimensionless probability, T and MaxIter are dimensionless counts, and ell-max carries the cost unit. The remainder vanishes when MaxIter is at least T log T, and the strongly-convex variant, Equation 18.5, sharpened to order epsilon, requires strong convexity in f, which zero-one loss itself does not satisfy; only its convex surrogates do. That is a real breakdown regime, not a footnote.

The Layer-2 binding into the 22-player football dynamical system is explicit and does not fabricate a football origin for these computer-science theorems. The visited-state distribution is the state variable; expert queryability is the constraint; the expert's recovery action is the information channel. A Coach-Mind policy trained only on successful historical drive states compounds errors when a sack or penalty pushes it into off-distribution third-and-long states; DAgger-style rehearsal of recovery from the learner's own visited states collapses the quadratic drive-collapse risk to linear. Telemetry calibrates this without any sportsbook odds: held-out action error epsilon, drive horizon T, worst single-play cost ell-max, iteration count MaxIter, and the covariate-shift gap between expert-visited and learner-visited states. The cross-layer veto is that a high-EV comfort call drawn from the expert distribution can be vetoed when the learner's internal state estimate says it is off-distribution; the physics of compounding error overrides the point estimate. This is the sovereign content: a finite mistake-bound, an error floor, and a tight T-squared-to-T separation, all dimensionally clean, all with explicit failure regimes.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The hidden state here is the compounding-error scar: SupervisedIL's T-squared bound was born from the historical failure of behavior-cloning agents that veer off the expert path and cannot recover. The self-driving-car wall example and the xor construction on p.215 encode that lineage. Ross, Gordon and Bagnell (2011) and Kaariainen (2006) are the cited ancestors of the imitation bounds. The perceptron's margin bound descends from Rosenblatt (1958) and the Novikoff convergence argument; the Bayes ceiling from classical statistical decision theory. Each primitive carries the scar of the failure mode that forced its assumption into existence.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: Under pressure the belief clash is three-way. The coach's comfort call is a policy drawn from the expert-visited distribution, high confidence because it matches historical success. The defensive coordinator's tendency trap is an adversarial perturbation that deliberately pushes the offense into off-distribution states, a disguised coverage that forces a sack, precisely the compounding-error trigger. The quarterback's internal clock is the learner's own state estimate, and it may signal that this is not a state it was trained on. Recursive modeling requires the quarterback to model the coordinator modeling the coach's comfort tendency, and to recognize that the highest-EV expert action is exactly the one the defense is baiting.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: The veto fires when the compounding-error physics overrides the point-estimate expected value. A comfort call with high expected value under the expert distribution can be vetoed because the learner's visited-state telemetry shows it is off-distribution: executing it risks a T-squared cascade, sack then third-and-long then drive collapse, rather than a linear-T cost. The psychological layer of coach confidence and the statistical layer of epsilon and covariate shift jointly veto the naive EV-maximizing action. The adjudication rule: prefer the DAgger-rehearsed recovery action whose loss scales linearly in T over the expert action whose worst-case loss scales quadratically, whenever the state-distribution gap exceeds threshold.

universal_lens: A polymath audit lens reads these four primitives as one template: a finite mistake-bound (perceptron), an unattainable optimality ceiling (Bayes), and a tight structural separation between two deployment regimes (T-squared vs T). The lens asks of any learned policy: what is its convergence guarantee, its error floor, and does its training distribution match its deployment distribution?
gsi_mapping: For GSI's clinical and biomechanical telemetry the isomorphism maps to motor-learning rehabilitation: a patient trained only on clinician-guided (expert) movement states compounds errors when fatigued into off-distribution joint-loading states. Aggregating recovery trials from the patient's own visited states (DAgger) reduces the quadratic fall-risk horizon to linear. Observables: per-rep movement error epsilon, trial horizon T, worst-load cost ell-max, and axonal/shear load telemetry. No odds.
gse_mapping: For GSE's Coach-Mind simulation and DFS/portfolio tail risk, the T-squared-to-T kernel is the compounding-error veto: a portfolio or drive-state policy trained on expert (winning) states fails quadratically when perturbed off-distribution. Dataset aggregation means stress-rehearsing recovery from the learner's own visited states. Telemetry: held-out action error, horizon, worst single-step loss, iteration count, covariate-shift gap. The engine queues but never publishes; no sportsbook odds as inputs.
